Performance outcome

The rider uses the brakes to control traction, speed and line, braking deliberately in the places where grip allows it and releasing where the tyres need their grip for turning, so they go faster overall.

Who it’s for

Fast riders who drag the brakes, brake in corners or skid, and racers looking for time in braking zones.

Before this lesson

  • Advanced Body Position.
  • Can ride the practice terrain in control at current pace.

Why it matters

Braking well is a speed skill. Riders who brake hard and briefly in the right places, then let the bike run, spend less time slow than riders who drag the brakes everywhere.

Technical model

Source check: d03 (video only: not yet watched). The reviewer must confirm this section against the original.

Brakes control grip as well as speed

Every tyre has a limited amount of grip, shared between braking, turning and accelerating. Braking hard while turning uses up grip the turn needs. Deliberate braking, before the corner or on the straightest, grippiest ground, saves grip for where it is needed.

Sometimes the answer isn’t more braking

If a rider is always on the brakes in a section, the better fix may be a different line or understanding where the traction is, rather than more brake.

Braking markers and release points

On a known section, riders choose where braking starts and where it stops. A coach can help mark these and check them on video. Markers change with conditions, so they are tools, not rules.

Front and rear brakes

Both brakes matter, and the balance changes with slope, surface, turn and suspension behaviour. Some coaches argue that riders often under-use the front brake on steep ground (see Technical Steeps). There is no universal ratio.

Physics & maths

The grip budget

A tyre’s grip can be pictured as a circle (the friction circle): the combined braking and cornering force can’t exceed about μN, the friction coefficient times the normal force. If braking uses most of it, little is left for turning. Braking also shifts load toward the front wheel, giving it more grip and the rear less, which is why rear-only braking skids easily.

A good Mathlete visual: a friction circle with a vector for braking and a vector for cornering; when their sum leaves the circle, the tyre slides.

Common errors

What you seePossible causesCorrection
Dragging the brakes all the way down a section.Nerves; not knowing where the grip is; no planned markers.Coach to supply
Braking in the corner instead of before it.Late vision; entry speed too high.Coach to supply
Rear wheel skidding into corners.Over-reliance on the rear brake; braking too hard where grip is low.Coach to supply
Braking on roots, rocks or wet patches.Braking where the rider happens to be rather than where grip is best.Coach to supply

Practice design

Setting
A known, coach-selected section with one or two clear braking zones, at below race pace.
Focus
Brake once, deliberately, in the chosen zone, then release completely; compare with the rider’s usual braking.
Feedback
Side footage of the braking zone and corner; segment timing if available.

Stop when

  • Conditions change (braking bumps, wet, loose).
  • The rider is braking later and harder rather than smarter.
  • Fatigue.

Video analysis

What the rider and coach look for in footage:

  • Where braking starts and ends relative to the planned markers.
  • Is the rider off the brakes before turn-in?
  • Skids or loss of line.
  • Time spent on the brakes per section (from video).
  • Exit speed or segment time.

Ready to move on

  • Coach-observed: deliberate braking zones and releases on a known section, consistently, without loss of control.

Educational checkpoints, not safety certificates.

Safety

Class 2: advanced riding skills. Needs the stated prerequisites, a controlled progression, suitable terrain and coaching guidance.

Practice only on terrain your coach has chosen, within your current skill, with the right protective equipment. Completing a lesson isn’t a safety certificate and doesn’t mean a rider is ready to try anything.
